name: Naive CD4 T cell
markers: CD45RA (human; mice use low CD44 instead to tell naive from memory)
summary: A helper T cell that has left the thymus but not yet met its antigen: a peptide held on MHC class II by antigen-presenting cells. It circulates between blood and lymph nodes looking for it. When a dendritic cell presents that peptide, it multiplies and specialises, becoming a Th1, Th2, Th17, Tfh or regulatory T cell.
functions: Patrols lymph nodes: it leaves the blood through high endothelial venules using CCR7 and CD62L, spends hours touching dendritic cells in the T-cell zone and, if it finds nothing, returns to the blood through the lymph.

Is activated only when three signals arrive together: its T-cell receptor binds the right peptide on MHC class II, CD28 binds CD80 or CD86 on the dendritic cell (co-stimulation), and cytokines set the direction.
Multiplies rapidly once activated (clonal expansion), driven partly by IL-2 that it makes itself, so the few cells that recognise an antigen become thousands.

Specialises according to the cytokines around it: IL-12 steers it to Th1, IL-4 to Th2, IL-6 with TGF-β to Th17, IL-6 and IL-21 to Tfh, and TGF-β with IL-2 to regulatory T cells. Much of this was worked out in mice; in humans the Th17 and Tfh signals differ.
Leaves behind memory T cells after an infection. Whether these pass through an effector stage first, and how fixed each helper fate is once chosen, are still debated.

Survives for years without meeting its antigen, kept alive by IL-7 and brief contacts with self-peptides. In adult humans the thymus shrinks and naive T cells are kept up mainly by slow division outside it; in mice the thymus stays the main source throughout life.
abundance: CD4 T cells make up roughly 30-60% of lymphocytes in adult human blood (about 0.5-1.5 × 10⁹ per litre). About half are naive in young adults, falling steadily with age. Laboratory mice, kept free of most infections, have few memory T cells, so most of their blood CD4 T cells are naive.
